course.title: Sitz Bath
course.splitRationale: The source runs about 3,400 words of narration - roughly 26 minutes. Its two section dividers (slides 2 and 12) name two sections, but its own menu names three topic groups, and those three are three different jobs for the learner: knowing when and why to use a sitz bath, performing it, and keeping it safe while teaching the patient. We followed the menu. Section 1 runs about 12 minutes, Section 2 about 11, and Section 3 about 7 - the shortest, but a complete and coherent unit rather than a tail bolted onto the procedure, which would have pushed Section 2 past 20 slides. Each package carries its own welcome, objectives, summary and results slide as this studio ships.
course.learningTimeNote: Indicative seat time to work through the module once, attentively: narration at 140 words per minute, plus 6s per panel the learner opens, plus per-question time for each knowledge check, plus a 10% allowance for pauses, replays and navigation. On-screen text is not counted separately because it is revealed in step with the narration that explains it.

smeQueries.issue: Slide 11 states the recommended water temperature as 40-45°C, the duration as 15-20 minutes and the frequency as 2-3 times a day, with no qualification. Slide 8 teaches a cold sitz bath ('cool or cold water ... for a short duration') and a medicated sitz bath, neither with any figure. As written the course tells the nurse the recommended temperature is 40-45°C and also that she will sometimes use cold water. The storyboard labels 40-45°C as the warm-bath figure. Please confirm that, and give the water temperature and duration for a cold sitz bath, and the solution, dilution and duration for a medicated one. A nurse asked to give a cold sitz bath currently has no parameters at all.

Slide 7 lists six items under one heading, 'Contraindications / Precautions', but they are not the same kind of thing: 'unconscious or uncooperative patient' is an absolute contraindication, 'impaired sensation' is a precaution, and 'very hot water' is a procedural hazard rather than a patient characteristic. The storyboard presents them in one table with a 'what the nurse does' column that distinguishes avoid from proceed-with-care. Please confirm which items are absolute contraindications in your practice.

Slide 13 is titled 'Preparation of Article' and its on-screen text lists the articles, but its speaker notes are the full procedure narration from slide 15, word for word. We have written the articles slide's voiceover from its own on-screen list, and carried the procedure narration on the procedure slides. Please review and confirm.

Slide 11 specifies 40-45°C; slide 14 says to check the temperature 'for tolerance by putting water on the back of the hand'. The back-of-hand test cannot distinguish 45°C from 50°C, which matters most for exactly the neuropathic patients slide 7 and slide 10 single out. Does policy require a bath thermometer, and if so where is it kept? The storyboard currently teaches both - measure where a thermometer is available, test on the back of the hand as a final check.

Two pieces of text appear to be leftovers from the deck this one was cloned from. 'Myocardial infarction' appears inside the slide 7 and slide 8 titles and in the slide 25 breadcrumb. A text box reading 'Abnormal muscle function' appears on slides 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21. Both have been excluded. Please confirm neither is intended content.

The deck's section dividers name two sections, while its menu names three topic groups - understanding the procedure, procedure and nursing care, and benefits and safety considerations. We have built three packages following the menu, because the third group is a different job for the learner. Please confirm the three-way split, or tell us if the two-section structure is the one the client expects.

Slide 20 names cross contamination as a complication and the aftercare slide says to clean the used equipment, but the course never states whether the sitz bath basin is single-patient-use or disinfected and reused, nor with what. Please state the local practice, including the disinfectant and contact time if the basin is reused.

The course teaches sitz baths after episiotomy and rectal surgery but never says how soon after delivery or surgery the first bath may be given, or for how many days it is typically continued. Patients going home are told to 'follow the prescribed frequency' without a default. Please supply the usual timing if there is one.

slides.title: What is a sitz bath?
slides.designRationale: One idea stated precisely, with the mechanism beside it. A definition slide rather than bullets, because everything later in the course - why it is indicated, why hot water is dangerous - follows from the learner knowing what the warm water actually does.

terms.description: A warm water bath the patient sits in to relieve discomfort in the perineal region
Warm water relaxes the anal sphincter and increases blood flow through the anal and perineal tissues
To enhance healing and relieve pain, while promoting comfort and relaxation

props.alt: Patient seated on a portable sitz bath basin, clinical, dignity preserved
props.searchTerms: sitz bath patient seated perineal care

candidates.note: Procedure photos - avoid anything exposing the patient

props.text: Increased blood flow is the whole mechanism. It is what promotes healing and reduces the pain, itching and irritation the patient feels.

slides.title: When a sitz bath is indicated
slides.designRationale: Seven conditions the learner must recognise on sight of a chart. Icons so they read as one scannable set, with the reasoning kept for the two slides that follow rather than crammed in here.
slides.devNotes: All seven reveal as one group on the second narration line - this slide is the overview; each condition is narrated in detail on the two that follow.

props.text: When a sitz bath is indicated

slides.title: Anorectal conditions
slides.designRationale: Four conditions, each with a different mechanism of relief - that is teaching content, not a list. A chip per condition with the reason behind it, so the learner can answer why rather than only when.

cards.title: Hemorrhoids
cards.body:
Swollen veins around the rectum.
Warm water relaxes the muscles, improves circulation and reduces inflammation.

cards.title: Anal fissure
cards.body:
A small tear in the anal lining.
The bath relaxes the sphincter, reduces spasm and speeds healing.

cards.title: Rectal surgery
cards.body:
Pain, swelling and irritation after the procedure.
The bath keeps the area hygienic and supports wound healing.

cards.title: Perianal abscess
cards.body:
Pus collecting near the anus.
The bath improves drainage and reduces inflammation.

slides.title: Postpartum and post-procedure
slides.designRationale: The obstetric and post-catheterisation indications grouped together, because the nursing context is the same - a comfort measure offered routinely rather than prescribed for a lesion.

cards.title: Episiotomy wound
cards.body:
A surgical incision in the perineum during delivery.
The bath keeps the area clean, reduces swelling and promotes healing.

cards.title: Postpartum perineal pain
cards.body:
Soreness and bruising after vaginal delivery.
Warm water relaxes the tissues and makes sitting and moving easier.

cards.title: Post-catheterisation discomfort
cards.body:
Irritation or soreness after urinary catheterisation.
The bath soothes the area and maintains local hygiene.

slides.title: Contraindications and precautions
slides.designRationale: Each item is only useful if the learner knows what could go wrong and what to do instead - genuinely two-dimensional, so a table. Written as prose in the source, which leaves the nurse to infer the risk from the name of the condition.

rows: Active bleeding
Warm water increases circulation and can worsen bleeding from the perineal or rectal area
Avoid, or proceed only on medical advice
Severe infection or deep wounds
Improper technique can spread infection or damage tissue
Seek medical evaluation before the procedure
Unconscious or uncooperative patient
The patient cannot report discomfort - risk of falls, burns and injury
Do not perform; the procedure needs cooperation
Allergy to medicated solution
Antiseptic or medicated additives can cause irritation, redness or an allergic reaction
Check allergies before adding any solution
Impaired sensation or neuropathy
A diabetic or neuropathic patient may not feel excessive heat
Assess temperature yourself; do not rely on the patient
Very hot water
Causes burns and tissue injury
Check the temperature every time, before the patient sits

props.text: A patient who cannot feel heat or cannot tell you about it is the one most likely to be burned. Assess the water yourself, every time.

slides.title: Three types of sitz bath
slides.designRationale: Type against effect against clinical use - the source gave type and description only, which does not tell the nurse when to choose each one. The third column is what makes the table decidable.

rows: Warm sitz bath
Improves circulation, relaxes muscles, reduces pain and swelling, promotes healing
Hemorrhoids, episiotomy wounds, anal fissure, postpartum discomfort. The most commonly used type
Cold sitz bath
Causes vasoconstriction, reducing inflammation, swelling and local edema
Immediately after injury or surgery, for a short duration. Use carefully - excessive cold is uncomfortable
Medicated sitz bath
Prescribed antiseptic or medicated solution reduces infection and cleanses the wound area
After rectal surgery or infection, and wounds needing special care. Only on medical advice

props.text: The type follows the goal. Warm to heal and relieve, cold to reduce swelling, medicated to control infection.

slides.title: Temperature, duration and frequency
slides.designRationale: Three numbers the nurse has to carry to the bedside. Given their own slide and their own icons rather than buried in a procedure list, because getting any of the three wrong is what causes the harm.

props.alt: Bath thermometer reading the temperature of water in a basin

candidates.note: Thermometer-in-water shots - prefer one where the scale is legible

props.text: Too hot burns. Too cold does nothing. Check the temperature before every single bath, not just the first one of the day.

slides.title: Section 1 in brief
slides.designRationale: A short recap in the order taught, consolidating the clinical reasoning before the procedure itself begins.

points: A sitz bath is a warm water bath for the perineal region - it relaxes the sphincter and increases blood flow.
That blood flow is what relieves pain, itching and irritation and promotes healing.
Indicated for hemorrhoids, episiotomy, postpartum pain, anal fissure, rectal surgery, perianal abscess, post-catheterisation.
Avoid or take care with active bleeding, severe infection, an uncooperative patient, allergy, and impaired sensation.
Three types: warm to heal and relieve, cold to reduce swelling, medicated to control infection.
Warm bath: 40– 45°C, 15–20 minutes, 2–3 times a day or as ordered.

slides.title: Performing the sitz bath
slides.designRationale: The core procedure, as a numbered track. The order is the content - privacy before exposure, water tested before the patient sits - and a track keeps that order visible while the detail is explored.

steps.label: Assess and take equipment to the bathroom or bedside
Fill the basin one-third full with warm water
Close the door or draw the curtains
Instruct the patient to expose the buttocks
Assist the patient to sit in the basin
Ask about comfort and water temperature
Remain with the patient or check frequently

layers.label: Assess and gather
lines: Take the equipment to the bathroom or the bedside, depending on the patient's mobility.

layers.label: Fill the basin
lines: One-third full, warm water at the recommended temperature.

layers.label: Provide privacy
lines: Close the door or draw the curtains around the patient.

layers.label: Expose the area
lines: Instruct the patient to expose the buttocks.

layers.label: Assist into the basin
lines: Support the patient into a sitting position; prevent falls.

layers.label: Confirm comfort
lines: Ask about comfort and whether the water temperature feels right.

layers.label: Stay or check often
lines: Watch for dizziness, irritation or any untoward reaction.

slides.title: If the patient is bedridden
slides.designRationale: A different technique for a different patient, not a footnote to the main procedure. Its own slide, because a nurse looking up how to treat a bedridden patient must not have to find it inside a step about something else.

items: Take an adequate amount of cotton roll or gauze
Soak it in warm water at the same recommended temperature
Place the wet cotton gently on the anal or perineal area
Replace and repeat as needed to maintain the warmth

candidates.note: Dressing trays - prefer one showing cotton and a bowl

props.text: The therapeutic effect comes from sustained warmth. A cooling compress left in place does nothing - replace it.

slides.title: Completing the procedure
slides.designRationale: The end of the treatment is where dizziness and falls happen, so the closing steps get their own track rather than being tacked onto the procedure slide.

steps.label: Continue the treatment for 20 minutes, or as prescribed
Assess continuously for any untoward reaction
Assist the patient out of the basin
Dry the area and apply a dressing if there is a wound
Make the patient comfortable

props.text: Patients can feel weak or dizzy standing up after a warm bath. Support them out of the basin and while they walk - do not leave them to manage it alone.

slides.title: Aftercare
slides.designRationale: Three tasks that happen after the patient is settled, and all three are infection control. Grouped on one slide so they read as a single closing routine rather than loose instructions.

items.label: Tidy the bed and position the patient

props.text: Assess the perineal area before you leave. If there is a wound or discharge, note its colour, amount and characteristics - you will need them for the record.

slides.title: What to document
slides.designRationale: Six specific fields, and the knowledge check that follows turns on knowing them. Treated as a named set rather than a sentence, because a nurse writing the note is checking off items.

props.text: Report any abnormal finding - redness, swelling, pain, bleeding or discharge - to the senior staff or physician immediately. The note is not the report.

slides.title: Learning objectives
slides.designRationale: Objectives for the closing section, pitched at recognising and preventing rather than reciting.

items.text: State the benefits of a sitz bath
Recognise the complications that can occur, and prevent each one
Demonstrate the nursing responsibilities that run through the procedure
Educate the patient on home care and safety measures

slides.title: What a sitz bath achieves
slides.designRationale: Six benefits, which is exactly the kind of list that becomes wallpaper as bullets. Icons give the eye six distinct things, and they are what the nurse repeats to a reluctant patient.

props.text: These are the reasons to give a patient who is reluctant. A sitz bath is uncomfortable to contemplate and easy to refuse - knowing what it achieves is what gets cooperation.

slides.title: Complications, and how to prevent them
slides.designRationale: Each complication has a cause and a specific preventive action, so the useful shape is three columns rather than a list of things that can go wrong. The prevention column is the one the nurse acts on.

props.text: Complications, and how to prevent them

rows: Burns
Water temperature too high
Check the temperature before every bath; never rely on the patient
Dizziness or fainting
Warmth and position change, usually getting in or out
Stay with the patient; assist in and out; support them while walking
Infection
Poor hygiene or improperly cleaned equipment
Hand hygiene, clean equipment, follow infection control practice
Skin irritation
Excessive heat, prolonged soaking, or allergy to a solution
Keep to the prescribed temperature and duration; check allergies
Cross contamination
Equipment not cleaned between patients
Disinfect the basin after every use; hand hygiene throughout

props.text: Every complication in this table is preventable by something the nurse does. None of them is bad luck.

slides.title: What you are responsible for
slides.designRationale: Six responsibilities spanning the whole procedure. Icons so they read as a checklist the nurse can run against themselves, which is how they will be assessed in practice.

props.text: Elderly and weak patients need assistance in and out of the basin every time, not only on the first treatment.

slides.title: What to teach the patient
slides.designRationale: The patient continues this treatment unsupervised, often at home. These five points are what they take away, so they get their own slide rather than a line inside nursing responsibilities.

items.label: Do not use very hot water

props.alt: Nurse explaining home care instructions to a patient before discharge

props.text: Teach this before discharge, not at the door. A patient who understands why hot water is dangerous will not test it at home.

slides.designRationale: Added. Complications are prevented by several habits at once, so a multi-select asks the learner to recognise a set rather than a single right answer - which is how prevention actually works.

props.stem: Which nursing actions reduce the risk of complications during a sitz bath? Select all that apply.

options.text: Checking the water temperature before every bath
Assisting the patient in and out of the basin
Extending the soak beyond the prescribed time if the patient finds it soothing
Disinfecting the basin between patients

props.rationale: A, B and D. Temperature checks prevent burns, assistance prevents falls from dizziness, and disinfection prevents cross contamination. Prolonged soaking causes skin irritation, so C increases risk rather than reducing it.

slides.title: Key points
slides.designRationale: The closing recap for the whole course, covering all three sections rather than this one alone, because this is where the learner finishes.

points: A sitz bath is a warm water bath for the perineal region that relieves pain and promotes healing.
Indicated for hemorrhoids, episiotomy, postpartum pain, anal fissure, rectal surgery and perianal abscess.
Assess for active bleeding, severe infection, impaired sensation and allergy before you start.
Warm, cold and medicated types - warm at 40–45°C for 15–20 minutes, 2–3 times a day.
Privacy, hand hygiene, correct technique and continuous monitoring are what make it safe.
Benefits: circulation, reduced edema, relaxation, pain relief, hygiene, wound healing.
Watch for burns, dizziness, infection, skin irritation and cross contamination.
Document accurately, and teach the patient before they continue at home.
